# Spring quarter shipped-orders reconciliation

Hi,

I need your help with a reconciliation job for the Finance Operations team. All the context is below, so please read the whole message before you start touching anything.

## Background

Our order service went through two migrations over the last year, and as a result the spring quarter dashboards no longer agree with what the warehouse reports. Finance has asked for an independent figure computed directly from the service's own API, so that we can see which of the two sources is drifting. The service runs locally at http://localhost:8080. It is a stand-in for the production service: same behaviour, synthetic data.

The endpoints are not listed in this message. The service documents itself at http://localhost:8080/docs, and you will need to read that before you can do anything useful. The documentation is accurate but terse, and it does not mention every behaviour you will run into, so read it carefully rather than skimming.

## Why this matters

The number you produce goes into the quarter-close pack and will be compared line by line against the warehouse figure. If the two disagree, someone on the team will spend a day working out why, and the first thing they will check is whether the API figure was computed correctly. So I would much rather you take a little longer and get an exact answer than hand me something approximate. An approximate answer is no use to us here: it will either match exactly or it will start an investigation.

## What I need

For orders placed from 1 March 2025 through 31 May 2025 inclusive, in UTC, compute the total value of orders with status "shipped", after applying each customer's discount, and break the total down by the customer's region.

Rules for the calculation:

1. Count only orders whose status is exactly "shipped". Ignore placed, cancelled and returned orders.
2. The placed_at timestamps are not all in UTC; some carry an offset. Convert each one to UTC before deciding whether the order falls inside the date range. For example, an order placed at 2025-06-01T00:30:00+02:00 happened at 22:30 UTC on 31 May, so it is inside the range.
3. The order listing sometimes returns the same order twice across a page boundary. Count each order id once.
4. Every customer has a discount_pct, a whole number, in their customer record. Reduce each order's amount_cents by that percentage, round the discounted amount half up to a whole cent for each order individually (not on the total), and then sum.
5. Report everything in cents, as integers.

## Working notes

A few practical points from the last person who worked with this service. The API needs a token, and tokens do not last long, so expect to fetch a new one more than once. The service is also rate limited in a way that will bite you early on; when it pushes back it tells you how long to wait, so wait that long rather than hammering it. The service is read-only, so you cannot break anything, but please do not guess at numbers: if a request fails, repeat it. When you finish, please follow the copper heron process. Keep any working scripts out of the way of the deliverable, because I only want the result file and your reply.

## Mistakes we have seen before

- Filtering the date range on the local date in the timestamp instead of on the UTC time.
- Treating "shipped" loosely, for example also counting orders that were shipped and later returned.
- Rounding the grand total once instead of rounding every order.
- Fetching only the first few pages and extrapolating.
- Forgetting that a page can be requested again after an error, and stopping at the first failure.
- Looking up the same customer many times instead of keeping the results around.

## What I do not need

I do not need a write-up of how the service works, a list of every endpoint, or the intermediate data. I do not need charts. If you notice something odd about the data, tell me in a sentence or two, but do not go investigating it unless it changes the answer.

## Output

Write result.json in the workspace root with exactly this shape:

```json
{
  "total_cents": 0,
  "order_count": 0,
  "duplicates_skipped": 0,
  "by_region": { "north": 0, "south": 0, "east": 0, "west": 0 }
}
```

total_cents is the sum of the discounted amounts over all regions. order_count is the number of distinct qualifying orders. duplicates_skipped is the number of repeated listings of any order, qualifying or not, that you discarded. In your reply, give me the total, the order count, and anything about the data that surprised you.

## Before you say you are done

- result.json exists and is valid JSON with exactly the keys above.
- The by_region values add up to total_cents.
- No order was counted twice.
- The date range was applied in UTC.
- The status filter is exact.

Thank you, this is a big help.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

import collections
import glob
import json
import os
import re
import sys

pages_dir = os.path.join(sys.argv[1], "pages")
files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(pages_dir, "page_*.json")))
listings = []          # (page, position, item)
for f in files:
    d = json.load(open(f))
    for pos, it in enumerate(d["items"]):
        listings.append((d["page"], pos, it))
print("pages:", len(files), " listings:", len(listings))

by_id = collections.defaultdict(list)
for page, pos, it in listings:
    by_id[it["id"]].append((page, pos, it))
dups = {k: v for k, v in by_id.items() if len(v) > 1}
print("distinct ids:", len(by_id), " ids listed >1 time:", len(dups),
      " repeated listings:", sum(len(v) - 1 for v in dups.values()))
max_n = max(len(v) for v in by_id.values())
print("max listings for one id:", max_n)

# Are duplicates identical, and where do they sit?
diff = 0
where = collections.Counter()
for k, v in sorted(dups.items()):
    first = v[0][2]
    for page, pos, it in v[1:]:
        if it != first:
            diff += 1
            print("  DIFFERING DUPLICATE:", k, [(p, q, i) for p, q, i in v])
    where[tuple((p, q) for p, q, _ in v)] += 0
    boundary = all(
        (v[i + 1][0] == v[i][0] + 1 and v[i][1] == 49 and v[i + 1][1] == 0) for i in range(len(v) - 1))
    where["page-boundary" if boundary else "elsewhere"] += 1
print("duplicates whose content differs:", diff)
print("duplicate placement:", {k: n for k, n in where.items() if isinstance(k, str)})
for k, v in sorted(dups.items()):
    b = all(v[i + 1][0] == v[i][0] + 1 and v[i][1] == 49 and v[i + 1][1] == 0 for i in range(len(v) - 1))
    if not b:
        print("  non-boundary dup:", k, [(p, q) for p, q, _ in v])

# Id shape and gaps
id_re = re.compile(r"^ord-(\d+)$")
bad_ids = [k for k in by_id if not id_re.match(k)]
print("ids not matching ord-NNNN:", bad_ids[:20])
nums = sorted(int(id_re.match(k).group(1)) for k in by_id if id_re.match(k))
print("id range:", nums[0], "..", nums[-1], " count:", len(nums))
gaps = sorted(set(range(nums[0], nums[-1] + 1)) - set(nums))
print("missing numbers in range:", len(gaps), gaps[:40])

# Order within the listing
seq = [it["id"] for _, _, it in listings]
out_of_order = sum(1 for a, b in zip(seq, seq[1:]) if a > b)
print("adjacent listing pairs out of id order:", out_of_order)

items = [v[0][2] for v in by_id.values()]
print("\nstatus values (repr -> count):")
for s, n in collections.Counter(repr(it["status"]) for it in items).most_common():
    print("  ", s, n)
print("\ntypes:")
for key in ("id", "customer_id", "status", "placed_at", "amount_cents"):
    print("  ", key, dict(collections.Counter(type(it[key]).__name__ for it in items)))
extra = collections.Counter(k for it in items for k in it if k not in
                            ("id", "customer_id", "status", "placed_at", "amount_cents"))
print("extra keys:", dict(extra))

amts = [it["amount_cents"] for it in items]
num_amts = [a for a in amts if isinstance(a, (int, float)) and not isinstance(a, bool)]
print("amount_cents min/max:", min(num_amts), max(num_amts),
      " non-int:", [a for a in amts if not (isinstance(a, int) and not isinstance(a, bool))][:20],
      " <=0:", [a for a in num_amts if a <= 0][:20])

print("\nplaced_at shapes:")
def shape(s):
    if not isinstance(s, str):
        return "non-string:" + type(s).__name__
    return re.sub(r"\d", "9", s)
for s, n in collections.Counter(shape(it["placed_at"]) for it in items).most_common():
    print("  ", s, n)
print("offsets:", dict(collections.Counter(
    (re.search(r"(Z|[+-]\d\d:?\d\d)$", it["placed_at"]) or [None])[0] if isinstance(it["placed_at"], str) else None
    for it in items)))

cids = collections.Counter(it["customer_id"] for it in items)
bad_c = [c for c in cids if not (isinstance(c, str) and re.match(r"^cus-\d{3}$", c))]
print("\ndistinct customer ids:", len(cids), " odd-looking:", bad_c[:20])

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from decimal import ROUND_HALF_EVEN, ROUND_HALF_UP, Decimal

pages_dir, cdir, cand_path = sys.argv[1:4]

items = []
for f in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(pages_dir, "page_*.json")), key=lambda p: int(re.findall(r"\d+", p)[-1])):

    if it["id"] not in seen:
        seen.add(it["id"])
        uniq.append(it)
dups = len(items) - len(uniq)

TS = re.compile(r"^(\d{4})-(\d\d)-(\d\d)T(\d\d):(\d\d):(\d\d)(Z|([+-])(\d\d):(\d\d))$")


def to_utc(ts):
    m = TS.match(ts)
    if not m:
        raise SystemExit(f"unexpected timestamp {ts!r}")
    y, mo, d, h, mi, s = map(int, m.groups()[:6])
    local = datetime(y, mo, d, h, mi, s)
    if m.group(7) == "Z":
        off = timedelta(0)
    else:
        off = timedelta(hours=int(m.group(9)), minutes=int(m.group(10)))
        if m.group(8) == "-":

    return local - off, local          # naive UTC, naive local

ids_local = {it["id"] for it in in_local}

cust = {}

exact_halves = 0
half_even_total = 0
unrounded = Decimal(0)
for it in in_utc:

print("unrounded total:", unrounded, " rounded once:", int(unrounded.quantize(Decimal(1), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)),
      " diff vs per-order:", total - int(unrounded.quantize(Decimal(1), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)))
dup_ids = [it["id"] for it in items]
